name: Edom
info: An Iron Age kingdom in the south of present-day Jordan, east of the Arabah, remembered for its copper mines, its god Qaus and its long rivalry with Israel and Judah in the Hebrew Bible.

facts.capital: Bozrah (now Busaira, Jordan), by the Hebrew Bible; Selah its principal stronghold in the time of Amaziah of Judah
facts.founder: Not known; Genesis 36 names Bela son of Beor as the first of the kings of Edom
facts.predecessor: Nomadic groups of the region, possibly the Shasu of the Egyptian records; by the Book of Genesis the Horites, displaced by Esau's descendants
facts.successor: Conquest by Nabonidus of Babylon; the Nabataean kingdom in the old land of Edom, and Idumaea in southern Judah, where the Edomites settled

t: Copper mining at Faynan and in the Timna Valley, dated to 1300–800 BCE, and the scale of the mines at Khirbat en-Nahas are read as evidence of a strong, centralized Edomite kingdom in the 10th century BCE.
Assyrian inscriptions name three kings of Edom, Kaus-malaka, Aya-ramu and Kaus-gabri, between about 745 and 680 BCE; the last unambiguous reference to Edom is an Assyrian inscription of 667 BCE.
After the fall of the kingdom in the 6th century BCE the Edomites settled in southern Judah, where they were known as Idumaeans; Herod the Great was of Edomite origin.
dyk: Qaus, the national god of Edom invoked in Edomite letters and personal names, is never mentioned in the Hebrew Bible, unlike the gods of other nearby nations; some scholars explain the silence by his close likeness to Yahweh.
ev: The earliest Iron Age settlements of Edom, possibly copper mining camps, are founded

sections.foundation:
Edom lay in the south of present-day Jordan, east of the Arabah, with the territory of Moab to its north; the Zered, now Wadi al-Hasa, marked the boundary between the two. The name comes from the Semitic root 'dm, meaning "man" and "red". Egyptian sources mention the land in the late Bronze Age: the list of the pharaoh Seti I from c. 1215 BCE, the chronicle of a campaign by Ramesses III, and a letter from a scribe at a border fortress in the Wadi Tumilat under Merneptah reporting "shasu-tribes of Edom" moving to watering holes in Egyptian territory. The Edomites may have been connected with the Shasu and Shutu, the nomadic raiders of those records.

The earliest Iron Age settlements, possibly copper mining camps, date to the 11th century BCE. Copper samples from the Timna Valley and Faynan, dated to 1300–800 BCE, led archaeologists under Ezra Ben-Yosef and Tom Levy to argue in 2019 that a kingdom already existed, against the view that the Arava held only a loose alliance of tribes. The Hebrew Bible makes the Edomites the descendants of Esau, who settled the land after displacing the Horites; it was also called the land of Seir, and Mount Seir may have been a cultic site.
sections.socioeconomy:
Copper was the basis of Edom's wealth. Mining and smelting in the Arava valley, at Faynan and in the Timna Valley, are dated to 1300–800 BCE, and the researchers who studied them concluded that Shoshenk I of Egypt, who attacked Jerusalem in the 10th century BCE, encouraged the trade and production of copper there instead of destroying the region. Settlement intensified by the late 8th century BCE, and the main sites so far excavated date between the 8th and 6th centuries BCE.

The Hebrew Bible gives Edom seaports at Eilat and Ezion-Geber, and places the "King's Highway" through its land. Genesis names the clans of Esau, among them Timnah, Teman and Kenaz, each with its families and locality, and the Torah calls their leaders aluf, a word it uses only for the dukes of Edom and Moab. The Edomite language was most similar to Biblical Hebrew and Moabite. The national god appears to have been Qaus, invoked in blessing formulas in letters and found in personal names; like other Levantine Semites the Edomites seem also to have worshipped El, Baal and 'Uzza. Edomite and Israelite religious practices evolved in parallel, and Victor Sasson has described an Edomite text that parallels the Book of Job.
sections.military:
Most of what is told of Edom's wars comes from the Hebrew Bible. When Moses and the Israelites asked to pass along the King's Highway, the king of Edom refused and prepared to resist, though he did not attack. The Edomites are next recorded as defeated by King Saul in the late 11th century BCE; forty years later King David and his general Joab defeated them in the "Valley of Salt", probably near the Dead Sea. An Edomite prince named Hadad escaped to Egypt, returned after David's death and failed in a rebellion. Edom then remained a vassal of Israel and, after the division of the kingdom, a dependency of Judah.

In the time of Jehoshaphat the inhabitants of Mount Seir are said to have invaded Judea with Ammon and Moab. Edom later revolted against Jehoram and elected a king of its own. Amaziah (796–769 BCE) defeated the Edomites and seized Selah, but by the biblical account the Israelites never subdued Edom completely. Egyptian inscriptions record that the "Aduma" at times extended their possessions to the borders of Egypt. When Nebuchadnezzar II took Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BCE, the Edomites may have helped plunder the city and slaughter the Judaeans, and Edom may have betrayed a treaty with Judah; Edomite settlement in southern Judah and the Negev had already begun, partly by military means.
sections.governance:
Assyrian cuneiform inscriptions call the land Údumi or Údumu and name three of its kings: Kaus-malaka in the time of Tiglath-pileser III (c. 745 BCE), Aya-ramu in that of Sennacherib (c. 705 BCE) and Kaus-gabri in that of Esarhaddon (c. 680 BCE). These are the kings known from sources outside the Bible; the last unambiguous reference to Edom is an Assyrian inscription of 667 BCE.

Genesis 36 lists eight kings who "reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the Israelites", from Bela son of Beor, whose city was Dinhabah, to Hadar, whose city was Pau. If the account may be taken at face value, the kingship was, at least in early times, not hereditary and perhaps elective. The First Book of Chronicles mentions both a king and chieftains. The Hebrew Bible names Bozrah, now Busaira in Jordan, as the ancient capital. For the periods of rule by Israel and Judah it describes governors or prefects placed over the Edomites by David, a form of government that seems to have continued under Solomon, and, in the time of Jehoshaphat (c. 870–849 BCE), a king of Edom who was probably a deputy appointed by the king of Judah. Edom's revolt against Jehoram ended that arrangement with a king elected by the Edomites themselves.
sections.impact:
The copper of the Arava was the ground on which archaeologists argued in 2019 that a kingdom could exist there in the 10th century BCE; Ben Yosef said the findings were consistent with the biblical story of an Edomite kingdom. In the Hebrew Bible Edom is the brother nation descended from Esau and also an enemy denounced by Isaiah, Jeremiah and Obadiah, perhaps for its part in the fall of Jerusalem. The Psalms say "over Edom will I cast out my shoe", and the Torah barred the descendants of a marriage between an Israelite and an Edomite from the congregation until the fourth generation, a law from which some early conversion laws in halacha were derived.

The Edomites outlived their kingdom. Settled in the hills south of Judea, they appear under the Greek name Idumaeans. Josephus says that John Hyrcanus I conquered Marisa and Adoraim and made the Idumaeans adopt Jewish law; some scholars have questioned the account since the late 1980s, though most historians still hold that it happened largely as he tells it. Antipater the Idumaean, progenitor of the Herodian dynasty, was of Idumean origin, and so was Herod the Great. In some Jewish traditions stemming from the Talmud, the descendants of Esau are the Romans.
sections.decline:
Edom flourished until the 8th century BCE and, after a period of decline, was destroyed by the Babylonians in the 6th. Its people had already begun to move west: excavations show Edomite settlement in the southern parts of Judah and in the Negev down to Timna before Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed the kingdom of Judah in 587/86 BCE, by peaceful penetration and by military means, taking advantage of Judah's weakness. Many Edomites migrated peacefully into southern Judea, a movement that continued under Nabonidus, whose conquest in the 6th century BCE ended Edom as a state. Nomadic tribes from the east pushed the Edomites further west; among them were the Nabataeans, who had established their own kingdom in what had been Edom by the first half of the 2nd century BCE.

In the Persian period the Edomites settled the southern hills of Judea down to north of Be'er Sheva, and the name Edom disappeared from the land east of the Arabah. Their new country was called Idumaea, by 365 BCE a truncated Persian province. Ostraca of the 4th century BCE show Arabs, Edomites, Judeans and Phoenicians living there, and settlement patterns and religious practice point to continuity with Iron Age Edom. After the Jewish–Roman wars, in which 20,000 Idumaeans joined the Zealots at the siege of Jerusalem in 70 CE according to Josephus, the Idumaean people disappear from written history.

summary: Edom was an Iron Age kingdom east of the Arabah whose copper mines at Faynan and Timna supported a centralized state by the 10th century BCE. Known from Egyptian, Assyrian and biblical sources, it fell to Babylon in the 6th century BCE, and its people lived on in southern Judah as the Idumaeans.
references: Bradley L. Crowell, Edom at the Edge of Empire: A Social and Political History (SBL Press, 2021)
Juan Manuel Tebes, "Edom and the Southern Jordan in the Iron Age", in Kyle H. Keimer and George A. Pierce (eds.), The Ancient Israelite World (Taylor & Francis, 2022)
Avraham Negev and Shimon Gibson (eds.), Archaeological Encyclopedia of the Holy Land (Continuum, 2001)

notes: The article gives no exact year for the end; 552 is the register's year. The article says only that Nabonidus conquered Edom in the 6th century BC, and elsewhere that the Babylonians destroyed it then.
The article's sentence on Nebuchadnezzar's destruction of 'the kingdom' in 587/86 BC is read here as Judah's kingdom, as the context (the weakened state of Judah) suggests.
Wars with Saul, David, Jehoram and Amaziah are told only as the Hebrew Bible's account; the -950 and -860 point years stand for the 10th century and the reign of Jehoshaphat.

The peak around 700-667 BCE follows the article's statement that settlement intensified by the late 8th century and that the main sites date 8th-6th centuries; the article also says the nation flourished 13th-8th centuries, so the peak could be placed earlier.
